text: This lab chains the two halves of the classical sandwich around a quantum circuit — data prep going in, result aggregation coming out — into one worked pipeline, the shape you'll actually write in production.

We'll build the pipeline as three independently testable units, catch two classic bugs using nothing but synthetic known-answer inputs, and see why that testing strategy matters even more here than in typical classical software.

Split the pipeline into normalize, which is a pure function with no network dependency; submit-and-wait, the only part that touches the real circuit, shaped like this real one from IBM Quantum; and aggregate, another pure function. Only the middle piece needs an integration test against a simulator or real backend.

Here are two known-answer tests you can run in milliseconds, with zero QPU cost. Feed normalize the vector two, two, two, two, and assert the output is exactly point five four times over. Feed aggregate a synthetic all-zeros count and assert plus one; all-ones, assert minus one. A normalization bug or a sign-convention bug fails one of these immediately — before ever touching a circuit.
This is real aggregated output from IBM Quantum's documentation — the exact shape the aggregate half of this pipeline produces and gets tested against.

And this is where it all actually gets written and tested — a real Amazon Braket notebook environment. In most classical pipelines, a bug like this looks obviously wrong. In a hybrid pipeline, a sign flip or bad normalization produces a plausible-looking number that's simply incorrect — which is exactly why testing against known answers, not real data, is the only reliable way to catch it before it corrupts an expensive run.
That closes out classical pre and post-processing. Chapter 3 moves into orchestration — what actually happens, in real measured time, between submitting a job and getting a result back.
